query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting Mo with additional Nb in the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo disordered BCC alloy will reduce the overall electronegativity difference and thereby relieve excessive lattice strain, leading to enhanced room‐temperature ductility while maintaining the high compressive yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy (Nb, Zr, Ti, Hf, Mo) exhibiting a compressive yield strength of ~1719 MPa but suffering from limited plasticity due to high Mo content.
generation.intervention: Reduce the fraction of Mo and correspondingly increase the Nb content (for example, replace a portion of Mo with Nb while keeping the other elements unchanged) to create a non‐equiatomic composition.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature compressive deformation using processing methods that yield a single-phase disordered BCC structure similar to the original alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: A solid solution with moderated lattice distortions and a lower overall electronegativity difference, without inducing secondary brittle phases.
generation.mechanism: Reducing Mo content lowers the average electronegativity difference among constituents, which decreases excessive lattice strain and facilitates dislocation mobility. This subtle change is expected to preserve the inherent solid solution strengthening provided by the refractory elements while enhancing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should display nearly the same high compressive yield strength (around 1719 MPa) as the original alloy but with a significantly improved compressive plastic strain (i.e. better ductility) at room temperature.
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy, which has a compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa but limited plasticity.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected as long as the Nb substitution does not exceed levels that might otherwise compromise the solid solution strengthening effect or lead to the precipitation of secondary phases; excessive Nb addition could lower strength if the balance of atomic size and bonding is perturbed.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Mo-to-Nb substitution ratio is not precisely defined. The quantitative trade-off between the improvement in ductility and any possible minor reduction in strength is uncertain and may depend on specific processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys in which Mo is progressively reduced and replaced by Nb (e.g., establishing Mo:Nb ratios of 100:0, 80:20, 60:40 relative to the base formulation) using the same processing route to maintain a disordered BCC single-phase structure. Perform room-temperature compressive tests and microstructural analysis.
measurements: Phase identification (via XRD and TEM) to confirm absence of deleterious precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-reduced, Nb-enhanced alloys either exhibit a significant drop in yield strength or do not show a measurable improvement in plasticity compared to the original equiatomic alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention.
